## Scientific method (conjecture, test, publish, repeat) `scientific_method`
- Deps: helped by empiricism_over_authority, controlled_trial, measurement_quantification, reproducibility_open_publication, fallibilism_provisional_knowledge
- Core idea: To test a claim about nature, state it precisely, work out what you should observe if it is true and if it is false, make the observation or design a comparison that distinguishes the predictions. Measure and record everything including failures, then let others repeat and criticise it. It works because it is a social error-correction process, not because any single person is unbiased. The cheapest way to convince is to predict something in advance that the old view does not predict (which of two pendulums swings faster, whether covered meat breeds maggots) and let the audience watch the outcome. It is a family of habits, not a fixed sequence of steps, and observation sciences (astronomy, anatomy) use it without laboratory experiments.
- Pitfalls: Presenting it as a fixed five-step recipe; real research moves back and forth between guess, test and revision | Saying 'science proves things': it eliminates errors and ranks explanations, the result stays open to revision | Claiming nobody tested anything before Bacon or Galileo, or that one person (Ibn al-Haytham, Bacon, Galileo) invented it | Staging a public demonstration that has not been rehearsed; one visible failure discredits the method and the player | Thinking experiments speak for themselves: without a clear rival hypothesis the audience fits any result into the old theory
- History: mesopotamia: c. 750 BC onwards – astronomical diaries: centuries of dated systematic observations used for prediction, without an explicit method of testing causes; china: c. 430–300 BC – the Mozi's 'three tests' of a doctrine (precedent, what people's eyes and ears report, practical benefit); c. 80 AD Wang Chong demands evidence and tests for claims; india: early centuries AD (dating disputed) – Nyaya Sutras classify the valid means of knowledge (perception, inference, comparison, testimony) and rules of debate; greece: 4th c. BC – Aristotle's systematic observation; 3rd c. BC Strato, Archimedes, Alexandrian physicians experiment; 2nd c. AD Ptolemy and Galen report experiments; islamic: early 11th c. – Ibn al-Haytham’s Book of Optics combines geometrical arguments with experiments using light, apertures and screens; europe: 13th c. Grosseteste and Roger Bacon praise experience (how far they experimented is disputed); 1600 Gilbert; 1620 Francis Bacon, Novum Organum; 1632–1638 Galileo; 1660 Royal Society; the word 'scientist' only 1833–1834 (Whewell)
- Read: Ibn al-Haytham, The Optics of Ibn al-Haytham, Books I–III: On Direct Vision (tr. A. I. Sabra, 1989) | Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620) | David Wootton, The Invention of Science: A New History of the Scientific Revolution (2015) | Peter Godfrey-Smith, Theory and Reality: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science (2003)

## Test claims instead of trusting authority `empiricism_over_authority`
- Deps: helped by printing_press
- Core idea: The age or fame of an author is no evidence for a claim about nature; what counts is whether anyone can check it. Old books contain checkable errors: Aristotle writes that women have fewer teeth than men (count them), and that a body ten times heavier falls ten times faster (drop a large and a small stone together); Galen relied heavily on animal dissection and inferred unseen passages through the wall between the heart's chambers. The persuasive form inside an older worldview is not 'Aristotle was a fool' but 'Aristotle and Galen themselves observed and told us to trust the senses over arguments; we are doing what they did, with more cases'. Authority remains a sensible shortcut where you cannot check, which is why testimony must be ranked, not ignored.
- Pitfalls: Claiming medieval scholars followed Aristotle blindly: scholastics disputed him constantly (Buridan, Oresme, the Paris condemnations of 1277) | Dismissing the authorities as stupid: Aristotle and Galen were excellent observers, and their opponents often had good arguments (no stellar parallax was measurable until 1838) | Attacking a university's or guild's textbook author in public attacks the livelihood of every local physician or master | Extending the argument to Scripture or to the classics of state ideology turns a dispute about nature into heresy or disloyalty | Asking people to distrust authority while demanding they trust the player without evidence
- History: india: by c. 8th c. AD – Carvaka materialists challenge scriptural authority and privilege perception; fragments quoted by critics show that some accepted inference grounded in ordinary experience; china: Warring States period – the Mozi lists what people have seen or heard among the tests of a doctrine; c. 80 AD Wang Chong, Lunheng, checks received stories against experience; greece: c. 350 BC – Aristotle: credit observation more than theories (Generation of Animals III.10); 2nd c. AD Galen urges readers to dissect for themselves; islamic: c. 900 – al-Razi, Doubts about Galen; early 11th c. Ibn al-Haytham, Doubts about Ptolemy (criticism of inherited astronomical models); c. 1200 Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi corrects Galen on the jawbone from skeletons in Egypt; europe: 1543 – Vesalius corrects Galen's anatomy from human dissection; 1660s Royal Society motto 'Nullius in verba' (take nobody's word for it)
- Read: Andreas Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica (1543) | Ramkrishna Bhattacharya, From Proto-materialism to Materialism: The Indian Scenario (2016) | David Wootton, The Invention of Science: A New History of the Scientific Revolution (2015)

## Controlled comparison (experiment with control group) `controlled_trial`
- Deps: helped by probability_statistics, measurement_quantification, placebo_blinding
- Core idea: To learn whether a remedy or method works, take cases that are as alike as possible, keep everything the same (place, food, care), give the treatment to one group and not to the other, decide in advance what you will count, and compare. Without a comparable group receiving usual care or another treatment, improvement may simply reflect natural recovery, which is why every healer honestly remembers cures. Allocation must not be chosen by the healer; cast lots (van Helmont proposed this in 1648), because people unconsciously give the new treatment to the stronger patients. Lind in 1747 took twelve scurvy patients in six pairs with the same diet and six different additions; after six days of citrus one was fit for duty and the other well enough to nurse the sick. More cases are needed the smaller the difference and the more variable the disease.
- Pitfalls: Comparing with the past or with another town instead of a control group treated at the same time | Letting the physician or patient choose who gets the treatment (selection bias); use lots | Drawing conclusions from two or three cases, or stopping the moment the result looks good | Believing Lind's trial settled the matter: he himself hedged, his boiled 'rob' of juice lost its potency, and the Royal Navy issued lemon juice only in 1795 | Withholding a known cure from the control group; the trial becomes a killing in the eyes of the families and the law
- History: mesopotamia: story set c. 600 BC at Nebuchadnezzar's court – Daniel 1: ten-day comparison of two diets (text written c. 2nd c. BC; literary, not a record); islamic: c. 900 – al-Razi reports bleeding one group of patients and deliberately not another to compare; 1025 Ibn Sina, Canon, sets conditions for testing a drug (simple disease, many cases, test on humans); china: 1061 – the Bencao Tujing compiled by Su Song recounts a traditional test of ginseng by having two men run, one with and one without it; europe: 1364 – Petrarch imagines comparing treated and untreated patients; 1648 van Helmont proposes allocation by lot; 1747 Lind's scurvy trial (published 1753); global: 1920s–1935 – R. A. Fisher, randomisation and design of experiments; 1948 British streptomycin trial uses a concealed random allocation schedule
- Read: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753) | Imogen Evans, Hazel Thornton & Iain Chalmers, Testing Treatments: Better Research for Better Healthcare (2006) | Ronald A. Fisher, The Design of Experiments (1935)

## Placebo effect and blinded trials `placebo_blinding`
- Deps: needs controlled_trial; helped by cognitive_biases
- Core idea: Patients who expect to improve report improvement, and physicians who expect it see it, so a fair test gives the comparison group a sham treatment that looks the same and keeps both patient and assessor ignorant of who received which. If outcomes are similar, the uncertainty around the difference determines how much benefit or harm the comparison can rule out. The classic demonstration is the French royal commission of 1784 on 'animal magnetism': a blindfolded subject had a crisis beside a tree the magnetiser had left untreated. It can be done anywhere with identical flasks numbered by a third person who keeps the key sealed.
- Pitfalls: Overstating the placebo effect: it changes how people feel and report (pain, nausea), it does not shrink tumours or cure infections | Mistaking natural recovery and regression to the mean for a placebo effect; only a no-treatment group separates them | Blinding the patient but not the person who judges the outcome | Exposing a respected healer, relic or exorcist by a sham test humiliates powerful people and can be read as impiety | Concluding that the patients were lying; their relief is sincere
- History: europe: 1599 – royal physicians test the supposedly possessed Marthe Brossier with sham holy water and relics; 1784 Franklin, Lavoisier and colleagues test mesmerism with blindfolds; 1799 Haygarth's wooden 'tractors'; 1835 Nuremberg salt test of homeopathy with shuffled, numbered vials; global: 1940s–1950s – double-blind randomised trials become the standard; 1955 Beecher, 'The Powerful Placebo' (its figures are now considered inflated)
- Read: Ted J. Kaptchuk, Intentional Ignorance: A History of Blind Assessment and Placebo Controls in Medicine (1998) | John Haygarth, Of the Imagination, as a Cause and as a Cure of Disorders of the Body (1800) | Ben Goldacre, Bad Science (2008)

## Correlation, causation and confounding `correlation_causation_confounding`
- Deps: helped by probability_statistics, controlled_trial, epidemiology_mapping
- Core idea: That two things occur together, or one after the other, does not show that one causes the other: the cause may run the other way, a third factor may produce both, or it may be chance. Fever follows swamp air, but the hidden third factor is the mosquito that breeds in the swamp; the patients of the most expensive physician die more often because he is called to the worst cases. To get from association to cause, compare groups that differ only in the suspected cause, look for a dose-response (more exposure, more effect), check that the cause comes first, and best of all intervene and see whether the effect follows. Snow's comparison of London households supplied by two water companies in 1854 is the model of a 'natural experiment' when you cannot intervene.
- Pitfalls: Reducing it to the slogan 'correlation is not causation' and then dismissing all observational evidence; correlation is a clue that needs explaining | Forgetting reverse causation and chance, and naming only confounders | Post hoc reasoning in one's own favour: the patient recovered after my remedy, the comet came before the king died | Assuming a bigger data set removes confounding; it only makes a biased answer more precise
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic writers warn against judging remedies from single outcomes; 'post hoc' fallacy catalogued by later logicians; islamic: 1025 – Ibn Sina's rules for drug testing require that the effect follow the drug constantly and that accidental causes be excluded; europe: 1620 Bacon's tables of presence, absence and degrees; 1739 Hume on causation as constant conjunction; 1843 Mill's methods of agreement and difference; 1855 Snow's water-company comparison; 1888 Galton defines correlation; global: 1950s–1965 – smoking and lung cancer studies; 1965 Bradford Hill's considerations for inferring causation
- Read: John Stuart Mill, A System of Logic (1843) | Austin Bradford Hill, The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation? (1965) | Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie, The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect (2018)

## Selection and survivorship bias, fair sampling `selection_bias_sampling`
- Deps: helped by probability_statistics, cognitive_biases
- Core idea: Conclusions drawn from the cases that happen to reach you are wrong when the way they reach you depends on the outcome. The temple shows the votive tablets of sailors saved after praying; as the ancient sceptic asked, where are the tablets of those who prayed and drowned? The healer hears from the cured, the astrologer is reminded of the hits, old buildings look well built because the bad ones fell down. The remedy is to count all cases, fixed in advance, including failures and those who never came back; and when you can only examine a part, to pick the part by lot so that every case has the same chance, which makes a small sample better than a huge self-selected one.
- Pitfalls: Thinking a large sample is automatically a good one (the 1936 Literary Digest poll had 2.4 million replies and was badly wrong) | Confusing 'random' with 'haphazard'; choosing 'typical' cases by eye reintroduces the bias | Telling the Abraham Wald bomber story with invented details; the core (armour where returning aircraft show no holes) is real, the dialogue is not | Counting only patients who completed a treatment and ignoring those who died or left
- History: greece: c. 420 BC – the votive-tablet reply attributed to Diagoras of Melos (also to Diogenes), reported by Cicero, De natura deorum III.89 (45 BC); india: Mahabharata (Nala episode, written form c. 400 BC–400 AD) – a king estimates the leaves and fruit on a tree from one branch; a literary hint of sampling, not a method; 1937 onwards Mahalanobis develops large-scale random sample surveys in Bengal; europe: 1620 – Bacon retells the votive-tablet story as the root of superstition (Novum Organum I.46); 1802 Laplace estimates the population of France from sample districts; 1895 Kiaer's 'representative method'; 1934 Neyman's theory of random sampling; americas: 1936 – Literary Digest poll fails, Gallup's much smaller sample succeeds; 1943 Wald's memoranda on aircraft damage
- Read: Cicero, De natura deorum III.89 | Abraham Wald, A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors (1943, reprinted 1980) | Darrell Huff, How to Lie with Statistics (1954)

## Measurement and quantification `measurement_quantification`
- Deps: helped by standard_weights_measures, arabic_numerals, precision_measurement
- Core idea: Replace 'hot', 'heavy', 'fast' and 'many' by numbers obtained with an instrument and an agreed unit: weigh, time, count and record in a table with date and place. Numbers let strangers compare results, reveal small regular effects that the senses miss, and expose wishful thinking. Every measurement has an error, so measure several times, report the spread, and never trust more digits than the instrument gives. Convincing examples are cheap: weigh a metal before and after calcining (it gains weight), weigh a patient, food and excreta as Santorio did, or count deaths by parish and week.
- Pitfalls: False precision: reporting six digits from a kitchen balance, or converting a rough guess into an exact-looking number | Measuring what is easy instead of what matters, then treating the number as the thing itself | Using local units without saying which: the foot, pound and bushel differ from town to town | Assuming earlier cultures did not measure: Babylonian, Chinese and Islamic astronomers and assayers measured with great care
- History: mesopotamia: 3rd millennium BC – standard weights and measures; c. 750 BC onwards dated numerical astronomical diaries; egypt: c. 3000 BC – royal cubit rods, Nilometers recording flood heights; china: 221 BC – Qin standardises weights, measures and axle widths; 9 AD bronze sliding caliper of Wang Mang's reign; greece: c. 240 BC – Eratosthenes measures the earth; c. 150 BC Hipparchus's star catalogue; islamic: c. 1020s – al-Biruni measures specific gravities of metals and gems and the earth's radius; 1121 al-Khazini, Book of the Balance of Wisdom; europe: 1450 – Nicholas of Cusa, De staticis experimentis, proposes weighing as the key to nature; c. 1580 Tycho's observations to about one arcminute; 1614 Santorio, De statica medicina
- Read: Nicholas of Cusa, Idiota de staticis experimentis (1450) | Alfred W. Crosby, The Measure of Reality: Quantification and Western Society, 1250–1600 (1997)

## Nature follows simple mathematical laws `mathematical_laws_of_nature`
- Deps: helped by measurement_quantification, geometry_proof, falling_bodies
- Core idea: Regularities in nature can be written as exact relations between measured quantities, and such relations predict cases never yet observed. Start with ones anyone can check: a string stopped at half its length sounds the octave, at two thirds the fifth; a lever balances when weight times distance is equal on both sides; a pendulum four times as long takes twice as long to swing; a ball rolling down a groove covers distances as 1, 4, 9, 16 in equal times. The trick that makes this work is idealisation: strip away friction and air, find the simple law, then add the disturbances back as corrections. The claim is not that qualities and purposes are unreal, only that asking 'how much' gives answers that can be tested and built upon.
- Pitfalls: Asserting that the laws are exact for real objects; they hold for idealised cases and must be corrected for friction, air and error | Quoting formulas (F = ma, E = mc²) without units, definitions or a way to check them, which is indistinguishable from numerology | Forgetting that mathematical astronomy already existed (Babylon, Ptolemy, Kerala, China); the new claim is that earthly physics is mathematical too | Numerology and Pythagorean mysticism are the nearest familiar idea; listeners will hear cosmic harmony, not measurement
- History: mesopotamia: c. 450–50 BC – arithmetical schemes predict lunar and planetary positions; greece: c. 500 BC – Pythagorean string ratios; c. 250 BC Archimedes' laws of the lever and of floating bodies; c. 150 AD Ptolemy; china: Han period – numerical harmonics of pitch pipes and calendar astronomy; little attempt to mathematise terrestrial motion; india: 499 – Aryabhata's computational astronomy; 14th–16th c. Kerala school; islamic: c. 1021 – Ibn al-Haytham combines geometry and experiment in optics; c. 1020s al-Biruni; 1121 al-Khazini on hydrostatics; europe: c. 1335 – Merton 'calculators' prove the mean-speed theorem; c. 1350 Oresme graphs changing quantities; 1623 Galileo: the book of nature is written in mathematics; 1638 law of fall; 1687 Newton's Principia
- Read: Galileo Galilei, Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze (1638) | E. J. Dijksterhuis, The Mechanization of the World Picture (1961) | Eugene P. Wigner, The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences (1960)

## Falsifiability (risky, testable predictions) `falsifiability`
- Deps: helped by scientific_method, formal_logic
- Core idea: A claim about the world is only informative if it forbids something, so that some possible observation would show it to be wrong. A thousand agreeing cases cannot prove 'all swans are white', one black swan refutes it; so look for the test most likely to fail, and say beforehand what result would make you give the idea up. An explanation that fits every outcome (the patient recovered because of the remedy, or died because it was given too late) explains nothing. The convincing move is a risky prediction made in public, like Halley's in 1705 that the comet of 1682 would return about the end of 1758.
- Pitfalls: Confusing 'falsifiable' with 'false' or 'falsified'; a good theory is falsifiable and has survived the attempts | Claiming one failed prediction kills a theory: the test also depends on instruments and side assumptions (Uranus's deviation led to Neptune, not to the end of Newton) | Presenting Popper's criterion as the agreed definition of science; philosophers and working scientists treat it as one useful test among others | Calling unfalsifiable statements meaningless or worthless; ethics, mathematics and religion are simply not empirical claims | Demanding that a diviner or priest name in advance what would prove him wrong is a public challenge to his office
- History: greece: c. 450 BC onwards – refutation by counterexample and reductio (Zeno, Socrates); applies to arguments, not yet to experiments; china: c. 80 AD – Wang Chong refutes omen and ghost beliefs by drawing consequences that do not occur; islamic: c. 1021 – Ibn al-Haytham designs experiments to decide between rival theories of vision; europe: 1620 – Bacon: 'the force of the negative instance is greater' (Novum Organum I.46); 1758 return of Halley's comet; 1919 eclipse test of general relativity; 1934 Popper, Logik der Forschung (English 1959)
- Read: Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1959) | Karl Popper, Conjectures and Refutations (1963) | Peter Godfrey-Smith, Theory and Reality: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science (2003)

## Fallibilism (all knowledge of nature is provisional) `fallibilism_provisional_knowledge`
- Deps: helped by scientific_method, bayesian_reasoning
- Core idea: Nothing about the natural world is known with final certainty; every claim is held with a degree of confidence that should follow the evidence and be revised when the evidence changes. This does not mean all opinions are equally good: some claims have survived so many attempts to refute them that doubting them is unreasonable, and later theories usually keep earlier ones as close approximations (a flat earth is nearly right for a field, a sphere for a voyage, a slightly flattened sphere for a geodesist). In practice: say how sure you are and why, state what would change your mind, and treat your own remembered schoolbook facts in the same way. For a time traveller this is also honesty, since half-remembered knowledge is exactly where confident errors hide.
- Pitfalls: Saying 'science has proved' or 'we now know for certain' | Sliding into relativism: 'everything is just a theory, so my guess is as good as yours' | Describing superseded theories as simply wrong; Ptolemy predicts planets well and Newton still builds bridges | Preaching universal doubt in a religious setting, where it is heard as doubt of revelation; limit the claim to knowledge of nature gained by the senses | Never committing: a patron needs a recommendation with honest odds, not a list of doubts
- History: greece: c. 500 BC – Xenophanes: no man knows the clear truth, but by seeking we find better; 2nd c. BC Carneades' degrees of plausibility; c. 200 AD Sextus Empiricus; india: c. 500 BC onwards – Jain doctrine of conditional assertion (syadvada); c. 200 AD Nagarjuna; c. 800 the sceptic Jayarasi; china: c. 300 BC – Zhuangzi on the limits of every standpoint; islamic: early 11th c. – in Doubts about Ptolemy Ibn al-Haytham urges the critic to question his own judgement; c. 1108 al-Ghazali, Deliverance from Error, examines the grounds of certainty; europe: 1562 – Sextus printed in Latin; 1580 Montaigne; 1739–1748 Hume's problem of induction; c. 1897 Peirce coins 'fallibilism'; 1934 Popper
- Read: Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism (c. 200) | Richard H. Popkin, The History of Scepticism: From Savonarola to Bayle (2003) | Isaac Asimov, The Relativity of Wrong (1988)

## Weighing evidence (base rates and Bayesian updating) `bayesian_reasoning`
- Deps: needs probability_statistics; helped by fallibilism_provisional_knowledge
- Core idea: How much a piece of evidence should move you depends on how much more likely it is if the claim is true than if it is false, and on how plausible the claim was before. If a disease affects 1 person in 1,000 and a sign appears in 99 % of the sick but also in 5 % of the healthy, then of 1,000 people about 1 sick and 50 healthy show the sign, so a person with the sign has only about a 2 % chance of being sick. Work it out with counted people rather than percentages and listeners follow easily. The same rule explains why a surprising claim needs strong evidence and why testimony for a miracle or a marvellous cure must be weighed against the frequency of error and deceit.
- Pitfalls: Confusing the chance of the evidence given the claim with the chance of the claim given the evidence (the prosecutor's fallacy) | Ignoring the base rate and treating a 'reliable' sign or test as near-certain proof | Assigning probability zero or one to anything, after which no evidence can ever change the belief | Dressing up a guess as a calculation by inventing the input numbers
- History: greece: 2nd c. BC – Carneades grades impressions by plausibility, without numbers; europe: 1748 – Hume's argument on testimony for miracles; 1763 Bayes's essay published by Richard Price; 1774 Laplace states the general rule and applies it widely; global: 1940–1941 – Turing uses sequential weighing of evidence against Enigma; 1950s onwards Bayesian statistics revived
- Read: Thomas Bayes, An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763) | Sharon Bertsch McGrayne, The Theory That Would Not Die (2011) | Gerd Gigerenzer, Reckoning with Risk: Learning to Live with Uncertainty (2002)

## Reproducibility and open publication `reproducibility_open_publication`
- Deps: helped by printing_press, scientific_journal, scientific_academy, patents
- Core idea: Describe materials, quantities, apparatus and failures so another investigator can check the reasoning or repeat the procedure. An independent replication strengthens the evidence; a unique historical event can still be checked against other records. Publishing openly trades the short-term advantage of a secret for credit, criticism that finds your errors, and the work of thousands who build on yours; secrets held by a guild or an adept die with their holders and cannot be checked. The institution that makes this rational for the individual is priority: whoever publishes first, dated and witnessed, gets the honour, and patents or prizes can protect the income.
- Pitfalls: Telling a craftsman to give away the secret his family lives on without offering priority, patent or patronage in return | Assuming everything should be published: fortification, ciphers and weapons are state secrets, and disclosing them is treason | Leaving out the 'obvious' practical details, so that nobody can repeat the result and it is dismissed | Believing a published result is therefore true; much published work fails replication | Calling the alchemists' secrecy mere fraud; it was also the normal way to protect craft property
- History: mesopotamia: 2nd–1st millennium BC – technical tablets (glass recipes, omen series) carry secrecy formulas restricting them to the initiated; china: 11th c. – Song government prints standard medical, agricultural and mathematical works; 1088 Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays record techniques openly; islamic: 8th–10th c. – translation movement and a commercial paper-book trade circulate science across the caliphate; europe: 1540 Biringuccio and 1556 Agricola print mining and metallurgy in plain terms; 1660 Boyle's fully described air-pump experiments; 1665 Journal des sçavans and Philosophical Transactions; global: 1942 – Merton describes the norms of science (common ownership of results, organised scepticism); 2010s 'replication crisis' in psychology and medicine
- Read: Pamela O. Long, Openness, Secrecy, Authorship: Technical Arts and the Culture of Knowledge from Antiquity to the Renaissance (2001) | Steven Shapin & Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985) | Robert K. Merton, The Sociology of Science: Theoretical and Empirical Investigations (1973)

## Systematic errors of human judgement (cognitive biases) `cognitive_biases`
- Deps: helped by controlled_trial
- Core idea: Human minds err in predictable directions: we notice and remember what confirms our belief (confirmation bias), see patterns and intentions in chance, judge frequency by vivid cases, anchor on the first number heard, and explain away our own failures. Being clever or honest does not protect anyone, which is why methods that do not rely on judgement are needed: write predictions down beforehand, count hits and misses, use controls and blinding, and invite an opponent to check. A quick demonstration is Wason's game: say that 2, 4, 6 follows a secret rule and let people test triples; many people try only cases that fit their guess and overlook rules that also fit those cases.
- Pitfalls: Believing that knowing about biases makes one immune; people readily see them in others only | Using 'you are biased' as an insult or a way to end an argument | Repeating famous findings that later failed replication (several social-priming results popularised in the 2000s) | Presenting a tidy catalogue of hundreds of named biases as settled science; the solid core is small
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Thucydides notes that people accept what they wish and reason away what they dislike; china: c. 250 BC – Xunzi, 'Dispelling Blindness', on how a partial view obscures the whole; india: early centuries AD – Nyaya Sutras list fallacious reasons and sophistical moves in debate; islamic: 1377 – Ibn Khaldun lists the causes of error in reports: partisanship, trust in transmitters, flattery of the powerful, ignorance of how things work; europe: 1620 – Bacon's four 'idols' of the mind; 1960 Wason's 2-4-6 task; 1974 Tversky & Kahneman, heuristics and biases
- Read: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum (1620) | Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (1974) | Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011)

## Formal logic (valid deduction and fallacies) `formal_logic`
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, boolean_logic
- Core idea: An argument is valid when its form guarantees that the conclusion is true if the premises are, whatever it is about: 'all A are B, all B are C, so all A are C'; 'if P then Q, and P, so Q'. Validity is separate from truth, so a valid argument with a false premise proves nothing, and logic alone gives no new facts about the world, only what is already contained in the premises. The practical use is to spot the common invalid forms: 'if P then Q, and Q, so P' (affirming the consequent, the form of most 'the omen came true' reasoning). Distinguish formal invalidity from defects such as assuming the very claim at issue: a circular argument can be valid but gives no independent reason to believe it. In Greek, Indian, Islamic and scholastic settings the audience already knows this art well, so the player gains by using it correctly rather than by teaching it.
- Pitfalls: Confusing valid with true, or thinking logic can settle questions of fact without observation | Lecturing a 15th-century university audience on syllogisms they know far better than the player | Calling every disliked argument a 'fallacy'; appeal to a qualified authority or to experience is not one | Claiming Aristotle's logic was wrong; it was correct but covered only part of what Stoic and modern logic handle
- History: greece: c. 350 BC – Aristotle's syllogistic (Prior Analytics); 3rd c. BC Chrysippus's propositional logic; india: early centuries AD (dating disputed) – Nyaya five-membered inference; c. 500 AD Dignaga's Buddhist logic; c. 13th–14th c. Gangesa develops Navya-Nyaya; china: c. 300 BC – Later Mohist Canons on definition, inference and disputation; the school fades from view in the early imperial period; islamic: 10th–11th c. – al-Farabi and Ibn Sina extend Aristotle with conditional and temporal logic; logic enters the madrasa curriculum; europe: 12th–14th c. – scholastic logic (Abelard, Peter of Spain, Ockham, Buridan); 1847–1854 Boole's algebra of logic; 1879 Frege's predicate logic
- Read: Aristotle, Prior Analytics (c. 350 BC) | William Kneale & Martha Kneale, The Development of Logic (1962) | A. C. Graham, Later Mohist Logic, Ethics and Science (1978)

## Parsimony (Occam's razor) `occams_razor`
- Deps: helped by formal_logic
- Core idea: Of two explanations that account for the same observations equally well, prefer the one that assumes fewer separate things, and do not add an entity or cause unless the evidence forces it. The reason is practical: every added assumption is another way of being wrong and makes the explanation harder to test, while a story with enough spare parts can fit anything. It is a rule for choosing what to test first, not a proof that the world is simple. Newton's version: admit no more causes than are true and sufficient to explain the appearances.
- Pitfalls: Misquoting it as 'the simplest explanation is usually true'; it only compares explanations that fit the facts equally well | Attributing 'entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity' to Ockham; that wording is John Punch's of 1639, and the name 'Occam's razor' dates from 1852 | Claiming Copernicus won because his system was simpler; it still needed about as many circles as Ptolemy's until Kepler's ellipses | Using it against God or spirits in front of theologians; Ockham himself used it within theology and exempted revealed truths
- History: greece: c. 350 BC – Aristotle: the demonstration from fewer postulates is superior (Posterior Analytics I.25); c. 150 AD Ptolemy prefers the simplest hypothesis that saves the phenomena; india: classical period – 'lightness' (laghava) of assumptions as a standard argument in Nyaya and Mimamsa debate; europe: c. 1320 – William of Ockham: 'plurality is never to be posited without necessity'; 1687 Newton's first rule of reasoning; 1852 the phrase 'Occam's razor' (William Hamilton)
- Read: William of Ockham, Summa logicae (c. 1323) | Elliott Sober, Ockham's Razors: A User's Manual (2015)

## Thought experiment `thought_experiment`
- Deps: helped by formal_logic
- Core idea: Imagine a precisely specified situation and reason out what must happen in order to expose a contradiction in a theory or to isolate what matters. Galileo's case against 'heavier falls faster': tie a light stone to a heavy one; the slow one should hold the fast one back, yet the pair is heavier and should fall faster, so the premise defeats itself. Another is his ship: below deck on a smoothly moving ship, drops still fall straight and flies fly alike in all directions, so steady motion cannot be felt and the earth may move. Such arguments cost nothing and work in any language, but they only show what follows from assumptions and should be followed by a real test.
- Pitfalls: Treating a thought experiment as proof about the world; in air a heavy ball does land slightly before a light one | Telling the Leaning Tower of Pisa drop as fact; it rests on a late account by Viviani, while Stevin and de Groot really dropped lead balls at Delft in 1586 | Smuggling modern intuitions (frictionless planes, empty space) into the set-up as if they were obvious to the listener | Mocking Aristotle: his rule describes bodies sinking through a resisting medium reasonably well
- History: greece: c. 450 BC – Zeno's paradoxes; c. 400 BC Archytas asks what happens when one stretches a hand beyond the edge of the universe; china: c. 300 BC – paradoxes of Hui Shi and Gongsun Long; Zhuangzi's butterfly dream; india: c. 100 BC–200 AD – the chariot argument about the self in the Questions of King Milinda; egypt: c. 530 AD – John Philoponus of Alexandria argues from actual drops that unequal weights fall almost together; islamic: c. 1020 – Ibn Sina's 'floating man' argument for self-awareness; europe: c. 1350–1377 – Buridan and Oresme argue about a rotating earth with arrows and ships; 1586 Stevin's chain on a prism; 1632–1638 Galileo; 1867 Maxwell's demon; 1897 Mach popularises the term 'Gedankenexperiment'
- Read: Galileo Galilei, Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo (1632) | James Robert Brown, The Laboratory of the Mind: Thought Experiments in the Natural Sciences (1991)

## Source criticism (testing documents and reports) `source_criticism`
- Deps: helped by empiricism_over_authority
- Core idea: A written or oral report is evidence only to the degree that its origin can be examined: who says it, how close were they to the event, what did they gain by saying it, do independent witnesses agree, and is it physically possible. Ten chronicles that copy one another are one witness. Forgeries betray themselves by anachronism: Lorenzo Valla showed in 1440 that the 'Donation of Constantine' uses Latin words, titles and place names that did not exist in Constantine's time. Ibn Khaldun's test is plausibility against how the world works: he challenges a reported Israelite army of over 600,000 by asking whether the territory could sustain so many fighters or allow them to manoeuvre.
- Pitfalls: Applying it aloud to Scripture, hadith, a dynasty's genealogy or a monastery's founding charter; that is heresy, treason or an attack on property titles | Arguing from silence: lack of surviving records is weak evidence that something did not happen | Assuming older means more reliable, or that a printed or officially sealed text must be true | Crediting Valla alone; Nicholas of Cusa (1433) and Reginald Pecock reached the same verdict on the Donation independently
- History: greece: c. 430 BC – Herodotus reports what is said without vouching for it; c. 400 BC Thucydides sets out his rules for testing eyewitnesses (I.20–22); china: c. 90 BC – Sima Qian compares sources and marks doubtful traditions; 710 Liu Zhiji, Shitong, the first treatise on critical historiography; late 17th c. Yan Ruoqu proves parts of the Book of Documents forged (evidential scholarship); islamic: 9th c. – hadith scholars grade reports by examining each chain of transmitters; c. 1030 al-Biruni's India; 1377 Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddimah; europe: 1440 – Valla on the Donation of Constantine (printed 1517); 1681 Mabillon founds the science of dating charters; 1670–1678 Spinoza and Richard Simon apply the method to the Bible; 1820s Ranke
- Read: Lorenzo Valla, De falso credita et ementita Constantini donatione (1440) | Ibn Khaldun, The Muqaddimah: An Introduction to History (tr. Franz Rosenthal, 1958) | Anthony Grafton, Forgers and Critics: Creativity and Duplicity in Western Scholarship (1990)

## Consent and ethics of experiments on people `informed_consent_research_ethics`
- Deps: helped by controlled_trial
- Core idea: Before trying an unproven treatment on a person, tell them what is known and what is risked and get their free agreement; do not experiment on those who cannot refuse (prisoners, slaves, orphans, the poor of a hospital) merely because they are available. Require prior evidence to justify the risks, independent review, a plan for monitoring harm and clear stopping rules. Respect withdrawal and record outcomes including deaths. Besides being right, this is what keeps a trial from ending in a riot or a murder charge and makes its results believed. The Hippocratic rule 'help, or at least do no harm' gives the argument a respected ancient footing.
- Pitfalls: Treating the consent of a master, parent, abbot or prince as the consent of the subject | Quoting 'first, do no harm' as part of the Hippocratic Oath; the wording comes from Epidemics I and the Latin tag is modern | Citing Jenner as a model: he inoculated an eight-year-old servant's son and then deliberately exposed him to smallpox | Heroic self-experiment as proof: one person is no trial, and a dead player teaches nobody
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic Oath and Epidemics I: act for the benefit of the sick, do no harm; india: c. 1st–2nd c. AD – oath of the medical student in the Charaka Samhita; china: c. 652 – Sun Simiao, 'On the Absolute Sincerity of Great Physicians': treat all patients alike, without regard to rank or reward; islamic: 9th c. – al-Ruhawi, Ethics of the Physician; europe: 1721 – smallpox inoculation tried on condemned Newgate prisoners in return for pardon; 1803 Percival, Medical Ethics; 1900 Prussian directive requiring consent; 1947 Nuremberg Code after the Doctors' Trial; americas: 1900 – Walter Reed's yellow fever volunteers sign written consent in Cuba; 1932–1972 Tuskegee syphilis study, the standard example of abuse; global: 1964 – Declaration of Helsinki
- Read: Nuremberg Military Tribunals, The Nuremberg Code (1947) | Albert R. Jonsen, A Short History of Medical Ethics (2000) | Susan E. Lederer, Subjected to Science: Human Experimentation in America before the Second World War (1995)

## Natural causes (naturalism about disease, weather, comets) `natural_causes`
- Deps: helped by eclipse_prediction, contagion_theory
- Core idea: Events such as disease, lightning, earthquakes, eclipses and comets follow regular causes that can be studied, predicted and sometimes prevented; they are not messages, punishments or the work of witches aimed at particular people. The strongest evidence is prediction and indifference: an eclipse can be calculated years ahead to the hour, lightning can strike exposed objects whether it is a church tower or a tree, plague kills the pious and the wicked in the same street. The framing that worked historically is 'secondary causes': God, Heaven or the gods work through a regular order of nature, and studying that order honours its author. The practical consequence is to stop looking for whom to blame and start looking for how it happens.
- Pitfalls: Presenting naturalism as atheism; nearly all its historical champions were believers, and the atheist framing gets the player prosecuted | Claiming natural explanations one does not actually have ('comets are just dirty snowballs') without being able to predict anything | Denying that an omen means anything to a court whose astrologers and diviners are state officials is an attack on the regime's legitimacy | Believing medieval scholars explained everything by miracle; scholastic natural philosophy sought natural causes as a matter of principle
- History: mesopotamia: c. 750 BC onwards – eclipses and planetary events are computed in advance, yet still read as omens for the king; greece: c. 585 BC – Thales and the Milesians explain earthquakes and lightning without gods; c. 400 BC Hippocratic 'On the Sacred Disease': epilepsy is no more divine than any other illness; china: c. 250 BC – Xunzi: Heaven's course is constant; rain follows the rain sacrifice just as it would without it; c. 80 AD Wang Chong: thunder is fire, not Heaven's anger; india: 499 – Aryabhata explains a lunar eclipse by the earth’s shadow and a solar eclipse by the moon obscuring the sun; later Carvaka authors reject appeals to supernatural agency; rome: c. 55 BC – Lucretius, De rerum natura; c. 65 AD Seneca, Natural Questions, treats comets as bodies with regular paths; islamic: 11th c. – Ibn Sina discusses uplift and erosion in mountain formation; al-Biruni infers from alluvial sediments that parts of the Indian plains were once under water; europe: c. 1120 – Adelard of Bath and William of Conches defend the search for natural causes; 1577 Tycho shows a comet lies beyond the moon; 1705 Halley predicts a comet's return; 1752 Franklin shows lightning is electricity
- Read: Hippocratic Corpus, On the Sacred Disease (c. 400 BC) | G. E. R. Lloyd, Magic, Reason and Experience (1979) | Wang Chong, Lun-Hêng (tr. Alfred Forke, 1907)

## Scepticism towards astrology, omens, witchcraft and transmutation `scepticism_superstition`
- Deps: helped by natural_causes, selection_bias_sampling, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Divination, astrology, witchcraft accusations and gold-making share one weakness: their successes are remembered and their failures explained away, and when hits and misses are all written down beforehand and counted they do no better than chance. Old and respectable arguments are available: twins born under the same stars have different fates, and thousands with different horoscopes die in one battle (Cicero, Augustine); confessions of witchcraft obtained by torture prove only that pain makes people say anything (Spee); no alchemist has ever sold gold cheaper than the mint. The fair test is to have the practitioner state specific predictions in writing, seal them, and compare. Be precise about alchemy: its transmutation of lead into gold fails, but its furnaces, acids and distillation are real chemistry.
- Pitfalls: Treating astrology as a fringe belief: in 1490 it is taught in medical faculties and practised at every court, and Tycho, Kepler and Galileo cast horoscopes | Calling the witch craze medieval; the great hunts fall about 1560–1650, and total executions are estimated at roughly 40,000–60,000, not millions | Denying the reality of witches where the Malleus Maleficarum (1486) calls that denial itself heresy; argue about proof and torture instead | Dismissing alchemists as frauds; they developed the laboratory methods chemistry inherited, and Boyle and Newton practised it | Ruining a court astrologer or diviner without offering the ruler something more useful makes a deadly, well-connected enemy
- History: mesopotamia: 2nd–1st millennium BC – omen series (Enuma Anu Enlil) are state science; horoscopes appear c. 410 BC; no known sceptical tradition; greece: 2nd c. BC – Carneades' arguments against astrology; c. 180 AD Lucian exposes the oracle-monger Alexander of Abonoteichus; rome: 44 BC – Cicero, De divinatione; c. 400 AD Augustine's twins argument; china: c. 250 BC – Xunzi: omens are rare natural events, to be wondered at but not feared; c. 80 AD Wang Chong, Lunheng, criticises claims that the dead harm the living, while accepting personal destiny; india: early Buddhist texts list divination among livelihoods monks should avoid; later sources preserve materialist criticisms of sacrificial rites attributed to the Carvakas; islamic: c. 1021 – Ibn Sina denies that alchemists can transmute species of metal; 1194 Maimonides' letter against astrology (written in Egypt); 1377 Ibn Khaldun refutes astrology and alchemy in the Muqaddimah; europe: c. 906 – Canon Episcopi calls night-flying a delusion; c. 1360s Oresme against divination; 1496 Pico della Mirandola's Disputations against astrology (Florence); 1563 Weyer; 1584 Scot; 1631 Spee, Cautio criminalis; global: 1985 – Carlson's double-blind test of astrologers in Nature finds chance-level results
- Read: Cicero, De divinatione (44 BC) | Keith Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) | Carl Sagan, The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark (1995)

## Atomism (matter is made of tiny particles in motion) `atomism`
- Deps: helped by atomic_theory, gas_laws, air_pump_vacuum
- Core idea: All matter consists of particles far too small to see, constantly moving, with empty space between them; the variety of substances comes from the kinds of particles and how they are arranged, and nothing is created from nothing or destroyed, only rearranged. Lucretius's everyday arguments still persuade: wet cloth dries and a smell crosses a room though nothing is seen to move, a ring wears thin over years, dust dances in a sunbeam, a drop of dye spreads through still water. A measurable hint of size: a teaspoon of oil calmed waves over roughly half an acre in Franklin’s report (1774). Dividing volume by area gives a film thickness of a few nanometres; using that to estimate molecular length requires assuming a single layer. Dalton’s atomic theory later connected particles to measurable combining ratios (1808).
- Pitfalls: Saying the Greeks 'discovered' atoms; they argued for them without evidence, and equally clever opponents argued against | Calling atoms indivisible little balls; chemical atoms have parts and are mostly empty space | Asserting the void to Aristotelians without a demonstration; 'nature abhors a vacuum' was the well-argued standard view | Forgetting the baggage: atomism was tied to Epicurus, denial of providence and the mortal soul, and after 1551 it was suspected of contradicting the doctrine of the Eucharist
- History: greece: c. 430 BC – Leucippus and Democritus; c. 300 BC Epicurus; rome: c. 55 BC – Lucretius, De rerum natura (rediscovered 1417 by Poggio Bracciolini, printed 1473); india: date uncertain, between c. 6th and 2nd c. BC – Kanada's Vaisheshika school teaches eternal atoms (paramanu); Jain and Buddhist authors also develop distinct atomisms; their chronological priority is uncertain; islamic: 9th–11th c. – some kalam theologians analyse bodies into indivisible atoms and hold that God continually recreates their properties; china: no sustained atomist school; matter is thought of as continuous qi (the Mohist 'end-point' is a geometric notion); europe: 1649 Gassendi revives Epicurus in Christian form; 1661 Boyle's corpuscles; 1808 Dalton; 1905–1909 Einstein and Perrin settle the reality of atoms through Brownian motion
- Read: Lucretius, De rerum natura (c. 55 BC) | Bernard Pullman, The Atom in the History of Human Thought (1998)

## The same physical laws on earth and in the heavens `universal_physical_laws`
- Deps: helped by telescope, universal_gravitation, falling_bodies, mathematical_laws_of_nature
- Core idea: The stars, planets and moon are made of ordinary matter and obey the same rules as stones and water here; there is no separate perfect, unchanging celestial realm. Evidence in rising order of force: new stars and comets show the heavens change (Tycho found their parallax too small for them to be atmospheric phenomena below the moon); a modest telescope shows mountains and shadows on the moon and spots on the sun; and the moon's orbit fits the same gravity that pulls an apple, weakened by the square of the distance (the moon is 60 earth radii away and falls 1/3600 as far per second as a stone does here). The pay-off is that experiments done on a bench tell us about the whole universe.
- Pitfalls: Assuming the earth-heaven divide was a religious dogma; it was Aristotle's physics, with good arguments, and Chinese cosmology never had it | Saying the Church forbade the idea that the heavens change; Jesuit astronomers confirmed Galileo's observations within a year | Offering the moon-and-apple calculation without the earth's size and the moon's distance, both of which the listener must accept first | Suggesting the sun is a burning stone to a society that worships it; Anaxagoras was prosecuted for impiety in Athens for that
- History: greece: c. 450 BC – Anaxagoras: the sun is a glowing stone and the moon is earthy; c. 350 BC Aristotle fixes the opposite view of a fifth, unchanging celestial element; egypt: c. 530 AD – John Philoponus of Alexandria argues that the heavens are made of ordinary, perishable matter; china: from 28 BC – court astronomers record sunspots, and 'guest stars' throughout; the heavens were never assumed changeless; islamic: c. 1000 – al-Biruni questions Aristotle's celestial physics in his correspondence with Ibn Sina; europe: 1572–1577 – Tycho's nova and comet; 1610 Galileo, Sidereus Nuncius; 1687 Newton unites celestial and terrestrial mechanics; 1859–1860 Kirchhoff and Bunsen find terrestrial elements in the sun's spectrum
- Read: Galileo Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius (1610) | Isaac Newton, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687) | Thomas S. Kuhn, The Copernican Revolution (1957)

## Mechanical philosophy (explain by matter and motion, not hidden purposes) `mechanical_philosophy`
- Deps: helped by atomism, mechanical_clock, blood_circulation
- Core idea: Explain a natural process the way one explains a clock or a mill: by the shapes, arrangement and motions of its parts pushing on each other, and ask 'how does it work' before 'what is it for'. An explanation by a named power (opium causes sleep because it has a 'dormitive virtue') only restates the question. The approach is convincing where a model can be built: the heart as a pump with valves, the eye as a dark chamber with a lens, the limbs as levers. It is a research programme, not the last word: gravity, magnetism and later fields act without pushing parts, and living things need chemistry and evolution as well as mechanics.
- Pitfalls: Concluding that animals are unfeeling machines, which historically excused cruel vivisection | Equating mechanism with godlessness; Boyle, Descartes and Newton saw the world-machine as evidence of its maker | Ridiculing purposes altogether; asking what an organ is for remains fruitful in anatomy (Harvey reasoned from the purpose of the vein valves) | Insisting everything works by contact; Newton's gravity was attacked by mechanists as an 'occult quality' and was right anyway
- History: greece: c. 430 BC – atomists explain all change by particles colliding; 3rd c. BC–1st c. AD Alexandrian mechanics and automata (Ctesibius, Hero); china: 1094 – Su Song's water-driven astronomical clock tower; cosmology stays organic rather than mechanical; islamic: c. 850 Banu Musa and 1206 al-Jazari build elaborate automata, without a mechanical philosophy of nature; europe: 1377 – Oresme compares the heavens to a clock; 1605 Kepler: the celestial machine is like clockwork; 1628 Harvey's heart as pump; 1644 Descartes, Principia philosophiae; 1660s Boyle names the 'mechanical philosophy'
- Read: René Descartes, Principia philosophiae (1644) | Robert Boyle, The Origine of Formes and Qualities (1666) | E. J. Dijksterhuis, The Mechanization of the World Picture (1961)

## Idea of progress (knowledge accumulates, the future can be better) `idea_of_progress`
- Deps: helped by reproducibility_open_publication, printing_press, systematic_invention
- Core idea: Knowledge and technique can grow without limit because each generation starts from what the last one recorded, so we can know more than the ancients without being wiser than they were; and with that knowledge, hunger, disease and toil can be reduced. The argument from visible evidence works best: things the revered ancients did not have (in 1490 the compass, gunpowder, printing, spectacles, mechanical clocks, paper) show that they did not know everything. Progress is neither automatic nor permanent; it depends on recording, teaching, open criticism and reward for improvement, and societies have lost skills before.
- Pitfalls: Claiming progress is inevitable or that newer is always better (the 'Whig' view of history) | Repeating the 'Dark Ages' myth; medieval Europe added mills, heavy ploughs, clocks, spectacles and universities | Confusing growth of knowledge with moral improvement; the 20th century had both antibiotics and industrial genocide | Telling a culture that reveres its sages or a golden age that they were ignorant; say instead that we see further by standing on their shoulders | Promising results on a timescale the patron will hold the player to
- History: greece: c. 500 BC – Xenophanes: the gods did not reveal everything at first, by seeking men find out better in time; rome: c. 65 AD – Seneca: a time will come when our descendants wonder that we did not know things so plain (Natural Questions VII); china: c. 240 BC – Han Feizi: new times need new measures, do not wait by the stump for another hare; the dominant Confucian view looks back to the sage kings; islamic: c. 900 – al-Razi: later scholars can surpass Galen because they inherit his work; 1377 Ibn Khaldun sees crafts and sciences accumulate within a civilisation but dynasties rise and fall in cycles; europe: c. 1120 – Bernard of Chartres, 'dwarfs on the shoulders of giants'; 1620–1627 Bacon, New Atlantis; 1687 onwards Quarrel of the Ancients and Moderns; 1750 Turgot; 1795 Condorcet
- Read: Condorcet, Esquisse d'un tableau historique des progrès de l'esprit humain (1795) | J. B. Bury, The Idea of Progress: An Inquiry into Its Origin and Growth (1920) | Joel Mokyr, A Culture of Growth: The Origins of the Modern Economy (2016)

## Invention as a method (organised research and development) `systematic_invention`
- Deps: helped by scientific_method, measurement_quantification, patents, industrial_research_lab
- Core idea: Inventions can be produced on purpose instead of waiting for luck or genius: state the need as a measurable target, collect what is already known, build small cheap models, vary one feature at a time and measure the result, keep a notebook of every trial including failures, and put people with different skills (a mathematician, a smith, a glassmaker) in one workshop with money and time. Smeaton found the best waterwheel in 1759 by testing model wheels on a bench; Edison's team tried thousands of filament materials; the Wright brothers tested about 200 wing shapes in a wind tunnel before building. The method needs a patron who accepts that most trials fail and is paid back by the few that work.
- Pitfalls: The lone-genius and 'eureka' story; Edison ran a staffed laboratory and did not invent the light bulb from nothing (Swan and others preceded him) | Blind trial and error without measurement or theory, which wastes years | Testing at full scale first; a failed full-size engine or bridge ends the patronage | Assuming an invention that works will be adopted; it must also be cheaper or better than what guilds and users already have
- History: egypt: 3rd c. BC – Ptolemaic Alexandria funds engineers who, by systematic trials, find the formula relating a catapult's spring diameter to its shot (reported by Philo of Byzantium, c. 200 BC); china: Han to Song – state workshops and arsenals with recorded specifications; improvement is organised but not as open-ended research; islamic: 1259 Maragha and 1420s Samarkand observatories as funded research institutes with staff, instruments and libraries; europe: 1576 – Tycho's Uraniborg; 1627 Bacon's fictional 'Salomon's House'; 1714 Longitude prize; 1759 Smeaton's model experiments; 1826 Liebig's teaching laboratory at Giessen; 1870s–1880s German dye-industry laboratories; americas: 1876 – Edison's Menlo Park laboratory; 1900 General Electric Research Laboratory; 1901 Wright brothers' wind tunnel; 1925 Bell Telephone Laboratories
- Read: Alfred North Whitehead, Science and the Modern World (1925) | Thomas P. Hughes, American Genesis: A Century of Invention and Technological Enthusiasm, 1870–1970 (1989) | Jon Gertner, The Idea Factory: Bell Labs and the Great Age of American Innovation (2012)

## Golden rule and universal ethics `golden_rule_universal_ethics`
- Core idea: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you; more generally, a rule of conduct is acceptable only if you would accept it when the positions are reversed. The rule needs no revelation and no shared religion, which is why it turns up independently in almost every literate culture, and it gives a stranger common moral ground in any era. Its radical step is the scope of 'others': extended beyond kin, city, faith and rank to every human being, it becomes an argument against slavery, persecution and cruelty. The player should quote the local version (Confucius, Hillel, the Gospel, a hadith) rather than import a foreign one.
- Pitfalls: Claiming it for one religion or presenting it as a modern discovery; every audience already has its own wording | Ignoring that tastes differ: the refined version asks what the other person would want, in their situation | Assuming that people who recite it apply it to outsiders, slaves, heretics or enemies; historically most did not | Equating it with Kant's categorical imperative, which Kant explicitly distinguished from it
- History: egypt: c. 1850 BC – Tale of the Eloquent Peasant has a reciprocity maxim (reading disputed); Late Period papyrus (c. 4th c. BC): 'that which you hate to be done to you, do not do to another'; china: c. 500 BC – Confucius: 'what you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others' (Analects 15.24); c. 430 BC Mozi's impartial care for all; india: c. 400 BC–400 AD – Mahabharata: do not do to another what is disagreeable to yourself; Buddhist and Jain texts likewise; greece: c. 4th c. BC – versions in Isocrates and attributed to earlier sages; mesopotamia: c. 20 BC – Hillel, trained in Babylonia: 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow' (recorded in the Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a); rome: 1st c. AD – Gospel form 'do to others as you would have them do to you' (Matthew 7:12); Seneca applies it to slaves; islamic: 7th c. – hadith: none of you believes until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself; europe: 1785 – Kant's universalisation test; the test asks whether a maxim could be a universal law; americas: 1993 – the Parliament of the World’s Religions in Chicago endorses the golden rule in its Declaration Toward a Global Ethic
- Read: Confucius, Analects 15.24 | Jeffrey Wattles, The Golden Rule (1996) | Harry J. Gensler, Ethics and the Golden Rule (2013)

## Human equality and dignity `human_equality_dignity`
- Deps: helped by golden_rule_universal_ethics
- Core idea: Every human being, whatever their birth, sex, colour, faith or rank, has the same basic worth and the same claim not to be owned, tortured or killed at another's pleasure. It is a moral claim about how people must be treated, not a factual claim that people are alike in strength or talent. Arguments that have worked: the capacities that matter (to suffer, to reason, to learn) are found in every class and people, as anyone can see when a slave's or peasant's child is taught; fortune is reversible, so today's master may be tomorrow's captive (Seneca); and nobody would accept rules of rank if they had to choose them before knowing where they would be born. Most traditions already hold a version before God or Heaven; the step is to draw the legal consequences.
- Pitfalls: Confusing equal dignity with equal ability or equal wealth, which listeners can refute at a glance | Citing the Cyrus Cylinder as the first human rights charter; it is conventional royal propaganda about restoring temples | Forgetting that the authors of 'all men are created equal' held slaves and excluded women; the idea was applied in stages | Preaching equality to peasants or slaves is incitement to revolt in every pre-modern state (1381, 1525) and is punished as such | Reading Pico's 'dignity of man' (1486) as a statement of equality; it is about human freedom to shape oneself
- History: china: c. 430 BC – Mozi: care for all impartially; c. 300 BC Mencius: anyone can become a sage; social hierarchy remains; india: c. 5th c. BC – the Buddha rejects worth by birth; a person is noble by conduct; caste persists in society; greece: c. 370 BC – Alcidamas: 'God has left all men free; nature has made no one a slave'; 3rd c. BC Stoic doctrine of one human community; rome: c. 65 AD – Seneca, Letter 47, on the humanity of slaves; c. 55 AD Paul: neither slave nor free, male nor female (Galatians 3:28); islamic: 632 – Farewell Sermon tradition: no superiority of Arab over non-Arab except in piety (wording transmitted in later collections); africa: c. 1236 – Manden Charter (Kurukan Fuga) of the Mali Empire, known from oral tradition first written down in the 20th c., dating and content disputed; 1615 Ahmad Baba of Timbuktu argues against enslavement on grounds of colour; americas: 1550–1551 – Las Casas defends the full humanity of the Indians at Valladolid; 1776 Declaration of Independence; 1791–1804 Haitian Revolution applies equality to the enslaved; europe: 1647 Putney Debates ('the poorest he'); 1673 Poullain de la Barre on the equality of the sexes; 1785 Kant: persons have dignity, not price; 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man; 1792 Wollstonecraft; global: 1948 – Universal Declaration of Human Rights
- Read: Seneca, Epistulae morales ad Lucilium 47 | Lynn Hunt, Inventing Human Rights: A History (2007) | United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)

## Natural (human) rights `natural_rights`
- Deps: helped by human_equality_dignity, rule_of_law
- Core idea: Each person has certain claims simply by being human (to life, to liberty of person, to the fruits of their labour, to a hearing before punishment) which no ruler granted and none may take away, and governments exist to protect them. They are not facts of nature like gravity; they are a moral and legal standard against which laws are judged, and their force comes from being written down and enforceable against the ruler in court. The persuasive bridge in older worlds is natural law, which Stoics, jurists and theologians already accept: if a higher law binds the king, then subjects have something they may demand, not merely hope for.
- Pitfalls: Treating natural law (duties under a higher order) and natural rights (claims of individuals) as the same thing | Calling Magna Carta (1215) a charter of universal rights; it secured privileges for barons and 'free men' | Asserting rights as self-evident to people whose moral language is duty, honour and status; translate into what the ruler may not do | Declaring that subjects may resist a ruler who violates rights is the theory of rebellion and is treated as treason | Listing modern rights (privacy, holidays, internet) as if all were equally basic
- History: greece: c. 441 BC – Sophocles' Antigone appeals to unwritten laws above the king's decree; 3rd c. BC Stoic natural law; rome: c. 51 BC – Cicero: true law is right reason in agreement with nature; jurists develop the 'law of nations'; china: c. 300 BC – Mencius: the people matter most, the ruler least, and a tyrant may be removed; a doctrine of rulers' duties, not individual rights; india: 3rd c. BC – Ashoka's edicts urge humane treatment of prisoners and subjects as royal duty (dharma), not as rights; islamic: c. 1100 – al-Ghazali: the law exists to protect religion, life, intellect, lineage and property; europe: 12th–14th c. canon lawyers and Ockham speak of subjective rights; 1539 Vitoria: the American Indians have true ownership and rule; 1625 Grotius; 1689 Locke; 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man; c. 1796 Bentham's rejoinder, 'nonsense upon stilts'; americas: 1776 – Virginia Declaration of Rights and Declaration of Independence; 1791 Bill of Rights
- Read: John Locke, Two Treatises of Government (1689) | Brian Tierney, The Idea of Natural Rights: Studies on Natural Rights, Natural Law and Church Law 1150–1625 (1997) | Lynn Hunt, Inventing Human Rights: A History (2007)

## Social contract (government by consent) `social_contract`
- Deps: helped by natural_rights, representative_government, written_constitution
- Core idea: Political authority is not owned by a family or handed down from heaven; it is a trust that people set up for their own protection, as if by an agreement: they obey common laws and a common judge, and in return the ruler keeps peace and justice. Locke treats a ruler who attacks the people as betraying that trust. For Hobbes the subjects covenant with one another to authorise a sovereign who is not a party to their agreement. The picture that convinces is the alternative: where everyone is judge in his own cause there is feud and insecurity, so everybody gains by a common authority, but only so long as it is better than what it replaced. It is a thought experiment about legitimacy, not a claim that such a meeting once took place.
- Pitfalls: Presenting it as history ('people once signed a contract') and being refuted by any chronicle | Forgetting that Hobbes used the same idea to justify near-absolute rule; the contract alone does not give liberty | Saying before a king that he rules by the people's consent and may be dismissed; this is exactly what regicides argued | Assuming it is purely modern or European; Mozi and Buddhist texts tell of a first ruler chosen to end disorder
- History: china: c. 4th c. BC – the Mozi (‘Identifying Upward’): before rulers each man had his own standard and there was chaos, so the worthiest was made Son of Heaven; india: c. 4th–3rd c. BC – Buddhist Aggañña Sutta: the people elect the first king (Mahasammata) and pay him in rice; Arthashastra 1.13: people made Manu king for a sixth of the grain; greece: c. 375 BC – Glaucon's account of justice as a compact (Plato, Republic II); c. 300 BC Epicurus: justice is an agreement not to harm; islamic: c. 1050 – al-Mawardi describes the caliphate as a contract concluded by pledge of allegiance (bay'a); europe: c. 1085 – Manegold of Lautenbach: a king who breaks his pact may be dismissed like a swineherd; 1579 Vindiciae contra tyrannos; 1651 Hobbes; 1689 Locke; 1762 Rousseau; americas: 1620 – Mayflower Compact; 1776 'governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed'
- Read: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651) | John Locke, Two Treatises of Government (1689) | Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Du contrat social (1762)

## Freedom of thought, speech and the press `freedom_of_speech_thought`
- Deps: helped by religious_tolerance, free_press, reproducibility_open_publication
- Core idea: People should be free to state and print opinions, including wrong and offensive ones, and to criticise those in power, without licence beforehand or punishment afterwards. The reasons (Milton, Mill): no censor is infallible, so suppression sometimes destroys a truth; even a false opinion forces the true one to be understood and defended rather than recited; and a ruler who silences criticism is the last to learn of famine, corruption and military failure. The ancient Chinese image is that stopping the people's mouths is like damming a river: it holds for a while and then breaks and drowns many. The freedom has always had limits at the edges (defamation, incitement to violence, military secrets); the principle is that the opinion itself is not the crime.
- Pitfalls: Presenting it as absolute, with no law of libel or incitement, which no society has ever had | Attributing 'I disapprove of what you say, but will defend to the death your right to say it' to Voltaire; Evelyn Beatrice Hall wrote it in 1906 | Idealising Athens, which executed Socrates, or Milton, who excluded Catholics from his tolerance | Asking a ruler for free speech as a right rather than as his own interest in honest counsel; and exercising it before it exists (blasphemy, sedition, lèse-majesté)
- History: greece: 5th c. BC – Athenian isegoria (equal right to address the assembly) and parrhesia (frank speech); 399 BC trial of Socrates shows the limits; china: text c. 4th c. BC about the 9th c. BC – Duke of Shao warns King Li that blocking the people's mouths is worse than blocking a river (Guoyu); remonstrance by officials becomes an institution; 213 BC Qin burning of books; india: c. 256 BC – Ashoka's edicts encourage sects to hear one another's teachings; 1575 Akbar opens a house of debate for Muslim scholars, later inviting participants from other faiths; islamic: 8th–10th c. – formal debates between schools and faiths at Abbasid courts, alongside episodes of enforced doctrine (the mihna, 833–848); europe: 1644 Milton, Areopagitica; 1670 Spinoza; 1695 English press licensing lapses; 1766 Swedish Freedom of the Press Act, the first such law; 1859 Mill, On Liberty; americas: 1791 – First Amendment to the United States Constitution
- Read: John Milton, Areopagitica (1644) | John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859) | Jacob Mchangama, Free Speech: A History from Socrates to Social Media (2022)

## Religious toleration and freedom of conscience `religious_tolerance`
- Deps: helped by freedom_of_speech_thought, secular_state
- Core idea: The state should not punish people for their beliefs or worship as long as they keep the peace. The arguments, in the order they usually work on rulers: persecution fails, because belief cannot be commanded and force produces hypocrites and exiles, not converts (Locke); it is costly, because the persecuted are often the most skilled craftsmen and merchants and other states gladly take them; it is dangerous, because every faith is a minority somewhere and the precedent returns; and no magistrate can be certain enough of doctrine to kill for it ('to kill a man is not to defend a doctrine, it is to kill a man', Castellio). Toleration as a grudging permit and freedom of conscience as an equal right are different stages, and most of history offers only the first.
- Pitfalls: Painting golden ages: Cyrus, al-Andalus, the Mongols and the Ottomans practised pragmatic, unequal toleration with taxes and restrictions, not equal rights | Saying the Edict of Milan (313) made Christianity the state religion; that was Theodosius in 380 | Forgetting that Locke himself excluded Catholics and atheists | Arguing that all religions are equally true (or false); that is heresy everywhere and is not needed for the case | Advocating it in Spain or Italy around 1490, where it marks the speaker as a suspected heretic or crypto-Jew
- History: mesopotamia: 539 BC – after taking Babylon, Cyrus claims in a royal inscription to have returned cult images and inhabitants to named settlements; india: c. 256 BC – Ashoka, Rock Edict XII: whoever praises his own sect and disparages others harms his own; 1564–1580s Akbar abolishes the tax on non-Muslims and proclaims 'peace with all'; china: Han onwards – Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism mostly coexist under state supervision, with episodes of suppression (845); rome: 311–313 – Edicts of Galerius and Milan grant freedom of worship; islamic: 7th c. onwards – protected (dhimmi) status for Jews and Christians in return for a tax and legal subordination; Ottoman millet system; east_asia: 13th c. – Mongol khans exempt clergy of all faiths and stage a public debate between religions (1254, reported by William of Rubruck); europe: 1554 Castellio against the burning of Servetus; 1568 Edict of Torda; 1573 Warsaw Confederation; 1598 Edict of Nantes (revoked 1685); 1689 Locke's Letter and the English Toleration Act; 1781 Joseph II's Patent of Toleration; americas: 1636 – Roger Williams founds Providence on liberty of conscience; 1786 Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom
- Read: John Locke, A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689) | Perez Zagorin, How the Idea of Religious Toleration Came to the West (2003) | Romila Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961)

## Secular state (separation of religious and civil authority) `secular_state`
- Deps: helped by religious_tolerance, rule_of_law
- Core idea: Civil government concerns peace, property and bodily safety and should neither enforce doctrine nor be controlled by clergy; religious bodies govern belief and worship by persuasion only, without the sword. Each side gains: the state is no longer torn by confessional wars or bound to one party's theology, and religion is no longer corrupted by office-seekers and used as a tool of rulers, which was Roger Williams's argument for the 'wall of separation'. A secular state is neutral between faiths, not hostile to faith. In Latin Christendom the starting point already exists in the distinction of the 'two powers' and in 'render unto Caesar'.
- Pitfalls: Equating secular with atheist or anti-religious | Calling medieval Europe a theocracy; popes and kings fought for centuries precisely because the two powers were distinct | Assuming one model: American separation, French laïcité and an established church with toleration (England) are different arrangements | Projecting 'church and state' onto societies without a church; in imperial China or the caliphates the issue is the ruler's control over ritual and scholars | Proposing it where the ruler's legitimacy is sacred (Mandate of Heaven, caliph, anointed king) removes the ground he stands on
- History: rome: 494 – Pope Gelasius I distinguishes priestly authority and royal power; china: from Han times – the state supervises and licenses religion; no independent church contests it; islamic: 9th c. onwards – in practice scholars (ulama) hold religious authority and sultans political power, without a doctrine of separation; 1924–1937 Turkish Republic adopts secularism; india: 1950 – Constitution of India establishes equal standing of religions (the word 'secular' added 1976); europe: 1075–1122 Investiture Controversy; 1324 Marsilius of Padua, Defensor pacis: clergy have no coercive power; 1689 Locke; 1905 French law on the separation of the churches and the state; americas: 1644 Roger Williams; 1786 Virginia Statute; 1791 First Amendment; 1802 Jefferson's 'wall of separation' letter
- Read: Marsilius of Padua, Defensor pacis (1324) | Roger Williams, The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution (1644) | Mark Lilla, The Stillborn God: Religion, Politics, and the Modern West (2007)

## Utilitarianism (judge rules by their consequences for everyone) `utilitarianism`
- Deps: helped by human_equality_dignity
- Core idea: Judge a law, custom or action by its effects on the well-being of everyone it touches, counting each person's happiness and suffering equally, and prefer what gives the greatest total good. Its power is as a tool of reform: it asks of every punishment, tax, privilege or ritual 'whom does this help, whom does it hurt, and by how much', and refuses the answer 'it has always been so'. Used as cost-benefit reasoning it speaks to rulers in terms of their own realm's prosperity, as Mozi did when he condemned aggressive war and lavish funerals as waste that feeds nobody.
- Pitfalls: Reducing it to 'the end justifies the means' or to personal pleasure-seeking | Ignoring the standard objection that a pure sum can justify sacrificing an innocent or a minority; most users combine it with rights | Pretending that happiness can be measured and added with precision | Forgetting to count everyone: applying the calculation to the listener's own class or nation only
- History: china: Warring States period – Mohist writers judge doctrines and policies by their benefit to all the people (wealth, population, order); an early consequentialist standard distinct from maximising pleasure; greece: c. 300 BC – Epicurus makes pleasure and freedom from pain the goal, but for the individual; india: c. 700 AD – Shantideva: the suffering of others is to be removed just like one's own; europe: 1725 Hutcheson: 'the greatest happiness for the greatest numbers'; 1764 Beccaria applies it to punishment; 1789 Bentham; 1863 Mill, Utilitarianism; 1874 Sidgwick
- Read: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789) | John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism (1863) | Ian Johnston (tr.), The Mozi: A Complete Translation (2010)

## Abolition of judicial torture; proportionate, certain punishment `abolition_of_torture`
- Deps: helped by habeas_corpus_fair_trial, utilitarianism
- Core idea: Torture to obtain confessions tests endurance, not guilt: the weak innocent confess and name others, the tough guilty go free, so every conviction it produces is worthless as evidence. Crime is deterred by the certainty and promptness of a moderate punishment far more than by the cruelty of a rare one, and public cruelty hardens the public. The argument must also offer a replacement: continental courts tortured because their law demanded a confession or two eyewitnesses for conviction, so abolition requires allowing judges to convict on a careful weighing of circumstantial evidence. Witch trials supply the proof, since tortured suspects everywhere confessed to impossible things.
