- Pitfalls: Thinking torture was lawless sadism; in Roman-canon procedure it was a regulated step that needed prior partial proof, so the law of proof must change too | Citing museum horrors such as the iron maiden, most of which are 19th-century fabrications | Calling it medieval; judicial torture peaked in the 16th–17th centuries and English common law largely did without it | Arguing only from mercy; magistrates respond to the argument that torture convicts the innocent and lets the guilty escape
- History: china: 167 BC – Emperor Wen of Han abolishes mutilating punishments; 7th c. Tang Code limits the amount and occasions of judicial beating; india: c. 250 BC – Ashoka’s Pillar Edict IV grants condemned prisoners three days before execution for appeals or religious observance; rome: c. 215 AD – Ulpian: evidence from torture is 'fragile and dangerous' (Digest 48.18.1.23), yet its use spreads; islamic: classical law – most jurists hold a confession under duress invalid; rulers' courts tortured nonetheless; europe: 866 Pope Nicholas I condemns confession by torture; c. 1250 torture enters continental procedure; 1631 Spee, Cautio criminalis; 1754 Prussia abolishes it; 1764 Beccaria; 1786 Tuscany abolishes torture and the death penalty
- Read: Cesare Beccaria, Dei delitti e delle pene (1764) | John H. Langbein, Torture and the Law of Proof: Europe and England in the Ancien Régime (1977) | Friedrich Spee, Cautio criminalis (1631)

## Positive-sum cooperation (trade is not zero-sum) `positive_sum_cooperation`
- Deps: helped by division_of_labour, comparative_advantage_free_trade
- Core idea: A voluntary exchange can benefit both sides: each expects to gain when agreeing to trade; wealth is therefore created by specialisation and trade, not merely moved from a loser to a winner. A worked example convinces: if a smith makes a knife in one day and a loaf's worth of grain in three, and a farmer the reverse, each gains two days by trading. The consequence for policy is that a neighbour's prosperity is an advantage (richer customers, more to buy), that plunder and monopoly destroy more than they capture, and that the ruler's revenue grows with the volume of trade he protects. Some contests really are zero-sum (a fixed piece of land, rank, a battle), and telling the two kinds apart is the skill.
- Pitfalls: Claiming everybody gains from every change; the gains are real in total but particular guilds, towns and workers lose | Asserting that trade makes war impossible; Angell argued in 1910 only that war had become unprofitable, and war came anyway | Confusing absolute with comparative advantage | Ignoring fraud, force and unequal bargaining, under which an exchange is not voluntary and the argument does not apply
- History: china: c. 90 BC – Sima Qian, 'Biographies of the Money-Makers': exchange arises of itself and enriches the state when left alone; greece: c. 360 BC – Xenophon and Plato note that specialisation and exchange supply the city's needs; rome: 4th c. AD – Libanius: God spread his gifts over different lands so that men would need and trade with one another; islamic: 1377 – Ibn Khaldun: cooperation and division of labour produce a surplus beyond the workers' needs; he argues that mounting tax demands can discourage productive activity and eventually reduce revenue; europe: 1748 Montesquieu on commerce softening manners; 1758 Hume, 'Of the Jealousy of Trade'; 1776 Adam Smith; 1817 Ricardo's comparative advantage; global: 1944 – von Neumann and Morgenstern distinguish zero-sum from non-zero-sum games
- Read: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776) | David Hume, Of the Jealousy of Trade (1758) | Robert Wright, Nonzero: The Logic of Human Destiny (2000)

## Game theory (prisoner's dilemma, credible commitment) `game_theory`
- Deps: helped by probability_statistics, positive_sum_cooperation, deterrence
- Core idea: When the result of your choice depends on what others choose, reason about their incentives as well as your own. The central case is the prisoner's dilemma: two parties each do better by cheating whatever the other does, so both cheat and both end worse off than if they had cooperated (two farmers who will not help with each other's harvest, two states arming). Cooperation can pay when future encounters are sufficiently likely and cheating jeopardises their rewards, when a third party enforces agreements, or when a side can bind itself visibly so that its promise or threat is believed (hostages, bonds, burning one's own bridges). Play it with coins for ten rounds and the audience discovers the logic themselves.
- Pitfalls: Concluding that people are selfish and cooperation is irrational; the lesson is which rules make cooperation stable | Applying one-shot reasoning to repeated dealings, or the reverse | Treating 'tit for tat' as the best strategy in all conditions; with mistakes and noise, more forgiving rules do better | Taking a Nash equilibrium for the best outcome; it is only a situation where nobody gains by changing alone | Repeating that Cortés burned his ships; he had them run aground and dismantled in 1519
- History: china: 207 BC – Xiang Yu sinks his boats and breaks the cooking pots before the battle of Julu, the classic commitment device (Shiji); c. 5th–4th c. BC Sunzi on shaping the enemy's choices; india: c. 3rd c. BC–3rd c. AD – Arthashastra's 'circle of kings' reasons about neighbours' and allies' incentives; mesopotamia: c. 3rd–5th c. AD – a Babylonian Talmud ruling on dividing an estate among creditors matches a modern game-theoretic solution (Aumann & Maschler, 1985); europe: 1651 Hobbes; 1713 Waldegrave's mixed strategy for a card game; 1740 Hume's two farmers; 1755 Rousseau's stag hunt; 1838 Cournot; americas: 1928–1944 – von Neumann, then von Neumann & Morgenstern; 1950 Nash equilibrium and the prisoner's dilemma (Flood, Dresher, Tucker); 1960 Schelling; 1980–1984 Axelrod's tournaments
- Read: John von Neumann & Oskar Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944) | Thomas C. Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict (1960) | Robert Axelrod, The Evolution of Cooperation (1984)

## Commons problem and how communities solve it `tragedy_of_the_commons`
- Deps: helped by game_theory, property_rights_land_registry
- Core idea: A resource open to all (pasture, forest, fishery, well, clean river) is overused, because each user gets the whole benefit of taking more while the damage is shared by everyone. It is nobody's wickedness, only the incentives, and it ends in ruin unless use is limited. Three kinds of remedy exist: private ownership, regulation by the state, and, often best, rules made and enforced by the users themselves: a defined membership, quotas matched to what the resource can bear (so many beasts per household, closed seasons, mesh sizes), mutual monitoring, graded fines and a cheap way to settle disputes. Mencius gave the conservation argument to a king around 300 BC: keep fine nets out of the ponds and axes out of the hills except in season, and there will be more fish and timber than can be used.
- Pitfalls: Repeating Hardin's claim that commons are always ruined; real village commons were regulated and many lasted for centuries (Ostrom) | Confusing a commons with rules and members with an unowned open-access resource | Offering only privatisation or state control; enclosure dispossesses the poor and provokes revolt | Adopting Hardin's own conclusions on coercive population control along with his metaphor
- History: greece: c. 330 BC – Aristotle: what is common to the most people gets the least care (Politics II.3); china: c. 300 BC – Mencius on closed seasons and net sizes (1A3) and the stripped Ox Mountain (6A8); islamic: 7th c. onwards – hima (reserved pastures) and detailed customary water-sharing rules; europe: medieval – village by-laws 'stint' the number of animals on the common; Swiss alpine commons documented from the 13th c.; Valencia's water tribunal; 1833 William Forster Lloyd's lectures; east_asia: Edo-period Japan – village common lands (iriai) with strict access rules; americas: 1968 – Hardin, 'The Tragedy of the Commons'; 1990 Ostrom, Governing the Commons
- Read: Garrett Hardin, The Tragedy of the Commons (1968) | Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action (1990) | William Forster Lloyd, Two Lectures on the Checks to Population (1833)
